context: linear structure · cut-and-cover box section by section, then tunnel MEP, then each utility moves in

brief.intro: New to this project type? A common utility tunnel is a walk-through concrete box under the road that houses many utilities together — power cables, water and chilled-water pipes, telecom, sometimes gas in a separate cell — on racks and supports, so they can be maintained and added to without digging up the street. Building it is like building a long basement: excavate, waterproof, cast the box section by section, backfill. Then the tunnel gets its own services (ventilation, lighting, drainage sumps, fire detection, access control), and only after that do the utility companies install their pipes and cables inside. It has to be finished before the road above, and it involves many owners whose approvals and installation slots all need to be scheduled.

glossary.plain: building the tunnel in an open excavation and then backfilling over it.
a separate chamber of the tunnel, e.g. one for power and one for water.
a strip cast into a concrete joint to stop water passing through it.
a steel channel set in the concrete so supports can be bolted on later without drilling.
a structure that brings fresh air in and lets warm air out of the tunnel.
a low pit that collects any water in the tunnel, with a pump to remove it.
a length of tunnel closed by fire doors so a fire cannot spread along it.
the authority or company that installs and operates one of the services in the tunnel.

must_get_right: Freeze the cross-section and each utility's space with all the owners first; a late change by one utility changes the concrete.
Treat it as a repetitive structure: plan bays in a cycle (excavate → blind → base → walls → top slab → waterproof → backfill) and count bays per week.
Cast-in channels, sleeves and openings must be in the formwork — coordinate the supports and penetrations before each pour.
Sequence the utilities inside: big pipes first while there is room, cables last; each owner needs a slot, an access and a handover date.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by tunnel bay (between movement joints) for the structure, and by tunnel section (between shafts) for MEP and utility installation.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar; dewatering runs continuously. Concrete in hot weather is planned for night pours.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Per bay: excavate → blind → base → walls → top slab → cure → waterproof → inspect → backfill. Per section: structure complete → racks and tunnel MEP → power-on → handover to utility owners → utilities installed → integrated test. The road above follows the backfill. The critical path normally runs through the structure cycle, then the utility owners' installation slots.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Utility owners agree the space allocation before design freeze and install in their agreed slots; existing services are diverted ahead of excavation; the road contractor follows the backfill.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: A long open excavation in a road corridor; limited access points for materials once the top slab is cast; confined-space rules inside the tunnel.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late agreement between utility owners, groundwater and leaks at joints, clashes at branch chambers, and owners installing late. Contingency is held before handover of the surface to the road works and before final handover.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by tunnel bay and section; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the structure cycle crews and each utility owner — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
